papers.title: Parameter Efficient Hybrid Transformer (PEHT) for Network Traffic Prediction via Dynamic Urban Congestion Integration
papers.authors: Abdolazim Rezaei, Mehdi Sookhak, Mahboobeh Haghparast
papers.abstract: Accurate network traffic prediction is a critical element for efficient resource allocation in dynamic urban cellular networks. However, prediction remains challenging because network demand is influenced by complex mobility patterns, congestion dynamics, and heterogeneous user behavior. This paper introduces the Parameter-Efficient Hybrid Transformer (PEHT), a network traffic prediction framework that integrates urban mobility and congestion information into a Transformer-based architecture. PEHT separates primary network communication features from secondary urban mobility features and incorporates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into the Transformer encoder to reduce the number of trainable parameters while maintaining high predictive accuracy. A multimodal fusion strategy then injects external mobility and congestion features into the decoder to improve traffic forecasting. Experiments on the Telecom Italia Milan dataset and multiple synthetic congestion scenarios show that PEHT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of RMSE, MAE, and $R^2$. The implementation is available in the GitHub repository.
takeaways: PEHT is a parameter-efficient Transformer framework for network traffic prediction that separates primary communication features from secondary urban mobility features and integrates dynamic congestion information.
It uses LoRA in the Transformer encoder and a multimodal fusion strategy in the decoder to inject mobility and congestion features while reducing trainable parameters.

Experiments on the Telecom Italia Milan dataset and synthetic congestion scenarios report better RMSE, MAE, and R^2 than state-of-the-art baselines, suggesting practical value for urban cellular resource allocation.
actionItems: Review the PEHT architecture details for how primary network communication features are separated from secondary urban mobility features and how LoRA is applied in the Transformer encoder.
Evaluate PEHT against your current network traffic prediction baseline on the Telecom Italia Milan dataset and compare RMSE, MAE, and R^2, including a check under synthetic congestion scenarios.
Assess whether the required mobility and congestion inputs are available and reliable in your deployment setting, since PEHT depends on external urban features for decoder fusion.

papers.title: HAT-4D: Lifting Monocular Video for 4D Multi-Object Interactions via Human-Agent Collaboration
papers.authors: Jiaxin Li, Yuxiang Wu, Zhenkai Zhang, Xinrui Shi, Haoyuan Wang, Yichen Zhao, Su Linxiang, Chenyang Yu, Mingyu Zhang, Yifan Ding, Boran Wen, Li Zhang, Ruiyang Liu, Yong-Lu Li
papers.abstract: Extracting dynamic 4D object interactions from massive, in-the-wild monocular videos offers a highly efficient data collection pathway for scaling Embodied AI and training VLAs. However, existing monocular 4D reconstruction methods primarily focus on isolated objects, often failing under the severe occlusions and complex dynamics inherent in multi-object interactions. To bridge this gap, we propose HAT-4D, the first agentic framework designed to reconstruct the 3D geometry, temporal dynamics, and physical interactions of multiple objects from a single video. By integrating VLMs with a multi-level human-in-the-loop feedback mechanism, HAT-4D efficiently resolves depth ambiguities and interaction-induced occlusions during 3D generation and 4D propagation, yielding physically plausible assets without relying on expensive multicamera rigs. As a scalable data engine, HAT-4D facilitates the creation of MVOIK-4D, an open-world benchmark for monocular 4D interaction reconstruction, accompanied by a novel multi-dimensional evaluation protocol focused on physical plausibility and temporal consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HAT-4D achieves SOTA performance on most evaluation metrics, while maintaining competitive semantic alignment. Ablation studies show that introducing a small amount of human feedback improves interaction reconstruction. Moreover, the data produced by HAT-4D effectively improves baseline performance when used for fine-tuning. Our data and code are available at https://lijiaxin0111.github.io/HAT4D/
takeaways: Introduces HAT-4D, an agentic framework for reconstructing 3D geometry, temporal dynamics, and physical interactions of multiple objects from a single monocular video.

Uses VLMs plus multi-level human-in-the-loop feedback to resolve depth ambiguities and occlusions during 3D generation and 4D propagation; reports SOTA on most metrics and improved results from a small amount of human feedback.

Provides a scalable data engine for embodied AI and VLA training by generating physically plausible 4D assets and the MVOIK-4D benchmark with evaluation for physical plausibility and temporal consistency.
actionItems: Review the HAT-4D paper’s agentic monocular 4D reconstruction pipeline, especially the VLM-guided human-in-the-loop steps for depth ambiguity and occlusion handling.
Evaluate whether a small amount of human feedback and the MVOIK-4D benchmark protocol materially improve physical plausibility and temporal consistency versus baseline monocular 4D methods.

Question the adoption fit for robotics and autonomous systems: how dependent is HAT-4D on human feedback and how transferable are its generated assets beyond the reported monocular interaction setting?

papers.title: From Black-Box to Clinical Insight: A Multi-Stage Explainable Framework for Speech-Based Cognitive Impairment Detection
papers.authors: Yasaman Haghbin, Sina Rashidi, Ali Zolnour, Fatemeh Taherinezhad, Ali Fartoot, Hossein Azadmaleki, James M Noble, Maryam Dadkhah, Maryam Zolnoori
papers.abstract: Speech-based cognitive impairment detection offers a noninvasive, accessible alternative to costly biomarker assays, yet transformer-based models remain clinically uninterpretable. We propose a multi-stage explainability framework that translates black-box transformer predictions into clinically grounded narratives by integrating SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based token attribution, theory-informed linguistic features, and a four-stage LLM reasoning pipeline using LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct. Built on the SpeechCARE-Adaptive Gating Network multimodal screening model (F1 = 72.11% on the NIA PREPARE benchmark), the framework maps model outputs to four cognitive-linguistic dimensions, including lexical richness, syntactic complexity, and semantic coherence. Physician evaluation on 70 stratified English samples demonstrated strong alignment with patient-level cognitive profiles, and a System Usability Scale score of 82/100 indicated high potential for clinical workflow integration.
takeaways: Proposes a multi-stage explainable framework that turns black-box speech-based cognitive impairment predictions into clinically grounded narratives by combining SHAP token attribution, theory-informed linguistic features, and a four-stage LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct reasoning pipeline.

Built on the SpeechCARE-Adaptive Gating Network multimodal screening model, the approach maps outputs to four cognitive-linguistic dimensions and is evaluated on NIA PREPARE, where the base model reports F1 = 72.11%; physician review of 70 stratified English samples showed strong alignment with patient-level cognitive profiles.
Practical implication: the framework aims to make speech-based cognitive screening more interpretable and usable in clinical workflows, supported by a System Usability Scale score of 82/100.
actionItems: Review the multi-stage explainability design to verify how SHAP token attributions, theory-informed linguistic features, and the four-stage LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct reasoning pipeline are combined to produce clinically grounded narratives.

Evaluate the framework on a larger, more diverse set of speech samples beyond the 70 stratified English cases, checking whether the physician-aligned explanations and cognitive-linguistic mappings remain consistent with the NIA PREPARE benchmark setting.

Ask whether the reported interpretability and usability gains are sufficient for clinical adoption given the base model’s F1 of 72.11% and the reliance on English-language samples and a specific screening model.

papers.title: ToxiREX: A Dataset on Toxic REasoning in ConteXt
papers.authors: Stefan F. Schouten, Ilia Markov, Piek Vossen
papers.abstract: We introduce a new, contextual, multilingual dataset called ToxiREX: Toxic REasoning in ConteXt. The dataset consists of threads of Reddit comments and structured characterizations of what the comments imply, following a systematic toxic reasoning schema developed in a previous paper. Using the schema allows us to capture and explain implicit and context-dependent toxicity, while supporting mappings to existing toxicity taxonomies. The dataset includes comments in six languages (English, Arabic, Turkish, Spanish, German, and Dutch), collected from posts connected to specific major events (e.g. the 2023 Turkey earthquakes; the Russian invasion of Ukraine). We describe the context-preserving preprocessing of the threads. We create a training set of 125 thousand comments which is annotated by a commercially available LLM, and a test set of just under three thousand comments that is annotated by native speakers. We show that apparent disagreements in the test set annotations often reflect defensible alternative interpretations rather than noise. Finally, we provide baseline results by prompting and fine-tuning language models. To produce these results, we develop evaluation strategies for our hierarchical, schema-based predictions. While models perform better than random, there remains a lot of room for improvement, showing the task to be challenging. ToxiREX is the first dataset to simultaneously incorporate multiple languages, conversational context, and implicit toxicity, while using the toxic reasoning schema for rich, structured annotations. Dataset available at: https://github.com/cltl/toxirex
takeaways: Introduces ToxiREX, a multilingual contextual dataset for toxic reasoning in Reddit threads, using a structured schema to capture implicit and context-dependent toxicity while mapping to existing toxicity taxonomies.

Builds a 125k-comment training set annotated by a commercial LLM and a ~3k-comment native-speaker test set; reports that some test disagreements reflect plausible alternative interpretations, and evaluates prompting/fine-tuning with hierarchical schema-based metrics.

Practical implication: ToxiREX provides a richer benchmark for studying implicit toxicity across six languages and event-based contexts, and the baseline results show the task is challenging with substantial room for improvement.
actionItems: Review the ToxiREX schema, context-preserving preprocessing, and hierarchical evaluation setup before relying on the benchmark for toxic reasoning experiments.
Run a comparative evaluation using the provided baseline prompting and fine-tuning approaches on the six-language test set, with attention to hierarchical schema-based metrics.
Ask whether the reported ambiguity in native-speaker annotations and the event-specific Reddit context limit how broadly ToxiREX should be adopted for toxicity modeling beyond its original settings.

papers.title: LLawCo: Learning Laws of Cooperation for Modeling Embodied Multi-Agent Behavior
papers.authors: Qinhong Zhou, Chuang Gan, Anoop Cherian
papers.abstract: Embodied agents operating in decentralized and partially observable environments have attracted growing attention in recent years. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based agents often exhibit behaviors that are misaligned with their partners or inconsistent with the environment state, leading to inefficient cooperation and poor task success. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework, Learning Laws of Cooperation (LLawCo), that enables embodied agents to autonomously align with both their partners and task objectives. Our framework allows agents to reflect on past failures to extract misaligned behavioral patterns, which are used to derive high-level behavioral laws, such as "Talk when necessary" and "Wait for partner." These laws are explicitly incorporated into the agents' chains of thought via supervised fine-tuning, aligning their reasoning with task requirements and the behavior of other agents. To evaluate our approach, we introduce PARTNR-Dialog, a large-scale multi-agent communicative and cooperative planning benchmark built on the PARTNR environment. Experiments on existing tasks and our new benchmark demonstrate significant improvements in cooperative efficiency and task success rates. Across four backbone LLMs, our method achieves average success rate improvements of 4.5% on the PARTNR-Dialog benchmark and 6.8% on the TDW-MAT benchmark over state-of-the-art open-source communicative agent frameworks. See the LLawCo project page for details: https://www.merl.com/research/highlights/LLawCo
takeaways: LLawCo proposes Learning Laws of Cooperation to help embodied multi-agent LLM agents align with partners and task objectives in decentralized, partially observable environments.

The framework reflects on past failures to extract misaligned patterns, turns them into high-level behavioral laws, and injects those laws into chain-of-thought via supervised fine-tuning; it is evaluated on the new PARTNR-Dialog benchmark and TDW-MAT.

For embodied cooperation tasks, the method aims to improve cooperative efficiency and task success, with reported average success-rate gains over state-of-the-art open-source communicative agent frameworks.
actionItems: Review the LLawCo method details for how failure reflections are converted into behavioral laws and inserted into chain-of-thought via supervised fine-tuning, especially for decentralized, partially observable embodied settings.

Run a targeted comparison on PARTNR-Dialog and TDW-MAT across the four backbone LLMs to verify the reported task success and cooperative efficiency gains against open-source communicative agent baselines.

Assess whether the approach depends on benchmark-specific communicative planning cues or assumes access to reliable failure traces and partner-state signals that may limit adoption in real embodied multi-agent systems.

papers.title: Dialogue to Detection: A Multimodal Hybrid NLP Pipeline for Insurance Fraud Detection
papers.authors: Muhammad Shakeel Akram, Amal Htait, Abdul Hamid Sadka, Emma Meisingseth, Karishma Jaitly
papers.abstract: Insurance fraud imposes substantial financial losses and operational inefficiencies, raising premiums and impacting trust among legitimate policyholders. Early detection at FNOL remains a persistent challenge. Existing approaches rely largely on private, text-only datasets, limiting progress on multimodal methods that integrate linguistic, behavioural, and speaker-based indicators. We introduce a synthetic multimodal framework that replicates FNOL conditions. It generates agent-customer dialogue transcripts and two-speaker audios, performs ASR and diarisation. Downstream modules combine NER, regex-based feature extraction, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings in a rule-based risk score to flag narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and cross-case voice repetition while balancing sensitivity and false positives. Dataset validation and component-level evaluations show stability and transfer potential, offering a reproducible baseline beyond text-only fraud detection.
takeaways: Introduces a synthetic multimodal FNOL fraud-detection framework that combines dialogue transcripts, two-speaker audio, ASR/diarisation, and a rule-based risk score to detect narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and repeated voices.

Validates the dataset and evaluates components, with results described as showing stability and transfer potential; the pipeline uses NER, regex feature extraction, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings.
Practical implication: provides a reproducible baseline for early insurance fraud detection that goes beyond text-only methods while aiming to balance sensitivity and false positives.
actionItems: Review the synthetic multimodal FNOL pipeline design, focusing on how dialogue transcripts, two-speaker audio, ASR/diarisation, NER, regex features, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings are combined into the rule-based risk score.

Evaluate the reported dataset validation and component-level results by checking whether the system actually improves detection of narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and cross-case voice repetition while maintaining sensitivity and false-positive balance.

Assess whether a synthetic, multimodal baseline for early insurance fraud detection is suitable for adoption in real FNOL workflows, given the low applicability and low reproducibility signals and the reliance on private text-only datasets as the comparison point.

papers.title: Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction
papers.authors: Chenguang Wang, Ming Li, Xinyue Zeng, Zhuochun Li, Hong Jiao, Tianyi Zhou, Dawei Zhou
papers.abstract: Predicting human item difficulty is central to educational assessment, where reliable estimates support fairness and effective test construction. Existing methods often depend on costly human calibration or item-level textual representations, providing limited evidence about the cognitive processes that make items difficult. We argue that difficulty should be viewed not only as a property of item text, but also as an observable consequence of the problem-solving burden an item induces. Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) offer scalable process evidence through reasoning traces, but such evidence must be structured to support interpretable modeling. To this end, we introduce Epi2Diff (Episode to Difficulty), a framework that maps LRM reasoning traces into cognitively grounded episode sequences. These episodes group trace segments into functional problem-solving states, enabling difficulty to be modeled through reasoning scale, effort allocation, and state transitions. Epi2Diff extracts compact episode-dynamic features and combines them with semantic item representations for human difficulty prediction. Experiments on four real-world human difficulty datasets show that Epi2Diff consistently outperforms strong baselines, including fine-tuned small language models, LLM in-context learning, and supervised LLM adaptation. On SAT-derived classification benchmarks, Epi2Diff achieves an 8.1% average relative gain over supervised LLM fine-tuning baselines. Further analyses show that harder items induce more effortful, iterative, and implementation-centered episode dynamics, rather than merely longer responses. These results demonstrate that cognitive episodes in LRM reasoning traces provide a predictive and interpretable process representation for human item difficulty, offering a new lens for educational measurement with reasoning models.
takeaways: Introduces Epi2Diff, which maps LLM reasoning traces into cognitively grounded episode sequences to model human item difficulty as a function of problem-solving burden, not just item text.

Uses compact episode-dynamic features plus semantic item representations; evaluated on four real-world difficulty datasets, where it outperforms strong baselines and reports an 8.1% average relative gain on SAT-derived classification benchmarks.

Suggests cognitive episodes in reasoning traces can provide interpretable process evidence for educational measurement, enabling more reliable and fairer item difficulty prediction for test construction.
actionItems: Review the Epi2Diff pipeline for how reasoning traces are segmented into cognitively grounded episode sequences and how episode-dynamic features are combined with semantic item representations.

Reproduce the reported comparisons on the four human difficulty datasets, including the SAT-derived classification benchmarks, and compare against fine-tuned small language models, LLM in-context learning, and supervised LLM adaptation baselines.
Assess whether the proposed process-based features are practical and stable enough for educational test construction, especially given the low evidence and low reproducibility signals.

papers.title: Parameter-Efficient Continuous-Variable Photonic Quantum Neural Networks for Edge Quantum AI: Demonstration in Oral Cancer Detection
papers.authors: Akshay Bhagwan Sonawane, Sophie Choe, Lakshman Tamil
papers.abstract: Early detection of oral cancer markedly improves clinical outcomes, yet specialized diagnostic tools remain scarce in low-resource settings. Smartphone-based screening is a scalable alternative but needs lightweight models that run within edge-hardware constraints. Hybrid classical-quantum architectures are emerging candidates for parameter-efficient learning, yet most rely on qubit hardware that needs cryogenic operation, unsuitable for edge deployment. Continuous-variable (CV) photonic quantum computing, which operates at room temperature, offers a complementary route. We investigate a hybrid classical-CV quantum classifier for oral cancer detection from smartphone images. The pipeline combines a MobileNetV1 feature extractor, principal component analysis to 16 dimensions, and a parameterized CV-QNN of displacement, interferometric, and Kerr gates on a photonic backend. We propose a simplified $Φ\circ D \circ U_1$ CV-QNN architecture that cuts trainable parameters 40-45% relative to the standard CV-QNN layer of Killoran et al. (2019a), and identify dimensionality-reduction and encoding-restriction strategies that mitigate barren plateaus, raising loss-gradient variance by roughly 58 orders of magnitude. Whether the simplified layer beats the full layer is width-dependent: the full layer holds a small but significant edge at two qumodes, whereas the simplified layer is significantly better at four qumodes using 44% fewer parameters. The strongest model, a four-qumode simplified CV-QNN with only 18 parameters, attains the highest validation AUC of all models, exceeds a 55-parameter classical baseline using 67% fewer parameters, and reaches 100% calibrated test accuracy across all seeds. These results support CV photonic quantum machine learning for parameter-efficient, room-temperature medical image classification and motivate progress toward edge quantum AI.
takeaways: Proposes a parameter-efficient hybrid classical–continuous-variable photonic quantum neural network for smartphone-based oral cancer image screening, including a simplified Φ∘D∘U1 CV-QNN that uses 40–45% fewer trainable parameters than a standard CV-QNN layer.

Uses MobileNetV1 features, PCA to 16 dimensions, and a photonic CV-QNN backend; reports that dimensionality reduction and encoding restrictions greatly increase loss-gradient variance, and that performance depends on qumode width.

In the reported experiment, a four-qumode simplified CV-QNN with 18 parameters achieved the best validation AUC and 100% calibrated test accuracy across seeds, suggesting room-temperature, edge-oriented quantum models could support low-resource medical image classification.
actionItems: Review the four-qumode simplified a6 D U1 CV-QNN setup against the standard CV-QNN layer, focusing on the reported 4045% parameter reduction and width-dependent performance on oral cancer smartphone-image classification.

Replicate the MobileNetV1 + PCA(16) + CV-QNN pipeline and compare the simplified versus full layer at 2 and 4 qumodes, checking validation AUC, test accuracy, and gradient-variance behavior under the stated dimensionality-reduction and encoding restrictions.

Question whether the reported room-temperature, edge-oriented gains will hold under the low-resource, smartphone-deployment setting and the paper's low reproducibility/applicability signals before planning adoption.
